        The June 18, 2026 Order addressed rehearing requests relating to the Commission’s

December 18, 2025 Order6 in this proceeding, concerning the Commission’s determination that

the existing Network Service in the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable for service to Co-

Located Load and requiring that three new forms of service be made available for Co-Located

Load: Firm Contract Demand Network Service (“FCD”); Non-Firm Contract Demand Network

Service (“NFCD”); and Interim Network Service. Exelon and FirstEnergy sought rehearing of that

order on January 16, 2026, which rehearing request was denied by operation of law when the

Commission did not rule by February 17, 2026. Exelon and FirstEnergy have submitted Petitions

for Review in the Third Circuit Court of Appeals on the issues where their rehearing was rejected.7

The June 18, 2026 Order does not alter the Commission’s finding on the issues pending in Exelon

and FirstEnergy’s submitted petitions for review; Exelon and FirstEnergy are not addressing those

issues further here, and the issues are instead before the Third Circuit.

Network Service offerings to loads served by BTMG. This rehearing addresses only the extension

of the new service options to load served by BTMG.

           II.        The Burden Under FPA Section 206 Has Not Been Met: The Existing Rate
                      Has Not Been Shown To Be Unjust And Unreasonable.

           The FPA requires that the rates and charges of a public utility “in connection with the

transmission or sale of electric energy subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, and all rules

and regulations affecting or pertaining to such rates or charges shall be just and reasonable.”8

“[A]ny such rate or charge that is not just and reasonable is . . . unlawful.”9 Under FPA section

206, the Commission may, by its own motion or upon complaint from a third party, remedy any

“rate [or] charge” or “any rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate [or] charge”

found to be “unjust [or] unreasonable.”10 “The burden of proving an unjust or unreasonable rate

rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—that is, the Commission or the third-party

complainant.”11 In other words, a respondent to a FPA section 206 complaint is not required to

make an affirmative showing that its existing rate is still just and reasonable.

Rather than honoring the states’ freedom and flexibility to exercise their jurisdiction over such

questions, the Commission’s new rule appears to create a new federal construct that defines the

extent and terms of service in such situations. That is, the Commission’s new rules leave it entirely

up to the customer to specify a contract demand service level that it will purportedly not exceed,

even if state law mandates that the local utility provide the customer with backup service in the

event of an outage. The Commission’s conclusion that the customer will not take additional service

lies in direct conflict with the states’ backup service mandates. The Commission does not have

authority under the FPA to dictate the terms of retail service in that fashion.

           Unlike wholesale demand response programs, which “allow[] any state regulatory body to

prohibit consumers in its retail market from taking part in wholesale demand response programs,”

thereby “not requir[ing] any “‘action[ ] that would violate State laws or regulations,’” the

Commission’s new forms of transmission services provide no such limitation.88 As the Supreme

Court has explained, however, “if indirect or tangential impacts on wholesale electricity rates

sufficed, FERC could regulate now in one industry, now in another, changing a vast array of rules

         As the Supreme Court explained, the FPA

                   “limit[s] FERC’s sale jurisdiction to that at wholesale,” reserving
                   regulatory authority over retail sales (as well as intrastate wholesale
